Apply basic business analysis frameworks to evaluate the usability, commercial viability, and customer experience of existing e-commerce websites and mobile platforms.
Analyze the managerial implications of security risks and payment systems to propose appropriate non-technical strategies for risk mitigation and consumer trust building.
Cultivate a professional awareness of legal compliance and ethical responsibility to address social and political issues arising within the digital trade environment.

EEC101.description: This course provides a comprehensive examination of the rapidly evolving digital marketplace through the tripartite lens of business, technology, and society. It establishes a theoretical framework for understanding how digital trade mechanisms have revolutionized traditional economic structures and continue to reshape global commerce.In this course, students will investigate the foundational elements of the digital economy, ranging from technical infrastructures and security protocols to complex business models. The curriculum requires learners to analyze critical strategies in digital marketing and supply chain management while simultaneously evaluating the ethical, social, and political implications inherent in online commerce. Through this rigorous inquiry, participants engage with the practical realities of online retail, content delivery, and collaborative commerce.Upon completion, participants will possess the analytical acumen necessary to evaluate diverse e-commerce initiatives and the technical insight required for establishing a robust digital presence. Graduates will emerge equipped with a strategic perspective that integrates commercial innovation with ethical responsibility, preparing them to effectively navigate and lead within the complexities of the global digital trade environment.

clos.details: Understand the brief history of, rationale for, and ethical considerations related to intercultural communication as a field of study, practice, and research.
Describe and analyse the key elements of intercultural communication, such as culture and identity; critically examine identity politics as well as prejudice and intolerance.
Understand the different channels of production and consumption of messages in intercultural communication: verbal, nonverbal, rhetorical, and mediated.

Consider the different intercultural contexts in which the channels of messages are used, as well as associated challenges: cross-cultural adjustment, relationships and conflict, politics, and organizations.
Critically examine the practical applications of the key concepts related to intercultural communication through analysis of real-life case studies.

EIC301.description:
Teaching Method: Offline.
< - This course serves as an introduction to the field of intercultural communication, the study of communication processes within and across different cultures and social groups. 
< - The course aims to develop English-major students' understanding of the key theories, concepts, approaches and practices of intercultural communication in the contemporary world.
< - Issues covered in the course include intercultural communication as embodied in culture, communication, identity; power, stereotyping, and prejudice; verbal, nonverbal, and rhetorical communication; intercultural competence and conflict, intercultural communication in politics, and intercultural communication in organizations. Throughout the course, students will be encouraged to reflect critically on the ways these issues relate to their personal experiences of cultural differences and communication behaviours. 
< - They will be able to apply these theories and practices in case studies with a view to identifying effective communicative strategies in intercultural interactions. 
< - This course provides English-major students with the opportunity to learn the theoretical foundations of the discipline as well as practical knowledge and skills to help them become effective and ethical communicator across multiple cultural contexts. >

clos.details: Identify key concepts and terminology used in tourism translation and interpretation
Explain the cultural nuances and their impact on translation and interpretation within the tourism industry
Apply appropriate translation techniques to effectively convert tourism-related texts from the source language to the target language
Interpret oral communications accurately in tourism contexts, ensuring clarity and cultural sensitivity
Evaluate the quality of translated and interpreted texts, identifying areas for improvement
Create culturally appropriate and accurate translations of promotional materials for the tourism industry
Demonstrate an awareness of and respect for cultural diversity in translation and interpretation task
Display professionalism and ethical behavior in translation and interpretation practices, particularly in tourism contexts
Commit to continuous learning and improvement in the field of tourism translation and interpretation

EIT401.description:
The course is designed to familiarize students with translation and interpretation in tourism. The course focuses on (1) interlingual translation of different types of tourism documents and (2) the interpreting practice of tourism. During the course, the lesson may be conducted in various forms including documents, news, traditional lectures, exhibitions, tours, field trips... 
After taking this course, students should be able to:
- Demonstrate a clear understanding terms used in tourism
- Clearly understand different types and formats of texts used in tourism
- Demonstrate a clear understanding of different types and settings of tourism interpretation
- Translate and interpret and news and documents in tourism from Vietnamese into English and vice-versa

clos.details: Identify and analyze key literary genres and elements (e.g., character, plot, theme, language, style) to understand how literary texts reflect and challenge societal norms.
Apply multiple analytical frameworks (text-oriented, reader-oriented, context-oriented, author-oriented) and close reading techniques to interpret literary works critically and independently.

Synthesize insights into structured academic and creative outputs, such as persuasive arguments, scripted performances (e.g., mock trials), and analytical essays, supported by appropriate use of MLA citation and secondary sources.
Develop empathy and critical awareness of diverse human experiences—particularly related to gender, power, and morality—through engagement with literary characters and ethical dilemmas.
Cultivate a reflective mindset by examining one’s own values in response to the social, cultural, and historical contexts embedded in literature.

ELA301.description:
-Objective: 
Introduce students to a variety of literary genres and their key characteristics.
Develop students’ ability to perform close readings of literary texts.
Enhance students’ critical thinking and analytical skills.
Foster students’ understanding of the relationship between literature and its historical, cultural, and social contexts.
Improve students’ written and oral communication skills through literary analysis.
Apply the students' understanding of literary analysis into projects.
-Description:This course provides a foundational understanding of literary analysis. Students will explore a diverse range of literary genres, including fiction, poetry, drama, and film. Through close reading and critical thinking, students will develop essential skills in interpreting and analyzing literary texts. 
The course emphasizes the development of analytical frameworks and the ability to identify and discuss key literary elements such as character, plot, setting, theme, style, and language. Students will also learn to situate literary works within their historical, cultural, and social contexts. By the end of the course, students will be equipped with the tools to engage in sophisticated literary analysis and articulate their interpretations effectively in written and oral forms through text-oriented, author-oriented, reader oriented, context-orriented approahces
-Teaching method:
Lecture, seminar, interview, Flipped-classroom format

clos.details: Understand the properties and characteristics of semiconductor materials and diodes, and apply diodes in practical circuit designs.
Explain the operation of Bipolar Junction Transistors (BJTs) and design and analyze BJT amplifier circuits.
Describe the operation of Field-Effect Transistors (FETs) and analyze their biasing configurations.
Investigate the functionality of operational amplifiers (Op-Amps) and design practical Op-Amp circuits for various applications.
Utilize simulation software to model, simulate, and analyze electronic circuits effectively.
Demonstrate proficiency in constructing and testing electronic circuits, while applying safety practices and responsibility in laboratory settings.
Integrate professional ethics, social responsibility, and environmental considerations into the selection, design, and lifecycle management of electronic components.

ELC201.description: This course equips students with comprehensive knowledge of electronic circuits, starting from the fundamentals of semiconductor materials and advancing to the design and analysis of amplifier, operational amplifier (Op-Amp), and signal conversion circuits. It covers essential topics including diodes, Bipolar Junction Transistors (BJTs), Field-Effect Transistors (FETs), analog-to-digital and digital-to-analog conversion, and the operation of timer circuits, with practical applications in circuit design. Through a combination of theoretical foundations and hands-on practice, students will develop skills to analyze circuit behavior, design efficient electronic systems, and utilize simulation software for modeling and testing. The course also emphasizes safety, professional ethics, and environmental considerations in electronic design.

Apply a range of digital technology tools to facilitate research processes and enhance writing quality effectively, critically, and responsibly.
Adhere to key principles of reseach ethics, such as beneficience, integrity, and respect of intellectual property, at every stage of the graduation project.
Present research procedures, findings, and analyses clearly, rigorously, and fluently in both written and verbal formats.
Develop autonomy and accountability in completing individual tasks and meeting all deadlines as set out in the project management plan.
Demonstrate strong interpersonal communication and effective collaborative working skills.
Reference source materials thoroughly and accurately, and formatted to relevant international standards.

ELP491.description:
Based on the study results of English language and specialized subjects in the previous semesters, students shall complete a Graduation project with the content and format appropriate to the research area to meet all course requirements. Thus, students are equipped with synthesis knowledge and skills associated with practice and theory about English and the subjects designed in the Program to build and implement the Graduation project.

Objectives of the course:
1) Help students consolidate and improve their ability to practice English in many aspects with specialized knowledge of each selected topic and exploit actual data in English to build a successful project.
2) Make English an effective tool for practical communication in their social environment.
3) Equip students with the ability to build and complete a project based on an idea of ​​the group, and practice teamwork skills.
4) Practice skills in judgment, analysis, selection and problem mining, data mining, technology-related knowledge, etc., to serve each type of project related to each selected topic array.
5) With the final report on project implementation, students also improve their ability to express themselves in English to present their ideas and working methods, present results, and use documents from a scientific perspective. 

Thus, they can pursue self-learning even after graduation and nurture the capability for expressing their own thoughts and ideas.

The Graduation project is conducted in GROUPS including 04 students (in case the students cannot be divided evenly, there can be a group of 3 or 5 students)

The instruction on the Graduation project is organized in two ways: in-class and in separate groups. The in-class instruction is conducted in the first week with the content regarding the rules, regulations, and things to be noticed during the process of writing the Graduation project. From week 2 onwards, the groups shall meet with the Project supervisor separately to discuss more in-depth about the group's topic.

The discussion with the Project supervisor can take place in many different forms appropriate to the availability of the supervisor and the students (meeting in class, online discussion, and email etc.). 

Project topic: the students can choose their topic in one of the following directions:
(1) Specialized English
(2) English in IT
(3) English in Economics and Trade
(4) Issues in applied linguistics
(5) Issues in English language teaching and learning

Students are required to attend at least 80% of scheduled meetings with their supervisor(s) to be eligible for the thesis or capstone defense.

ELR301.description:
This course provides a comprehensive foundation in research design and proposal writing, guiding students in developing the conceptual understanding and practical skills necessary to craft a sound research proposal. Students will explore the philosophical underpinnings and methodological distinctions among qualitative, quantitative, and mixed methods approaches, integrating this knowledge into the formulation of coherent research designs. Emphasis is placed on conducting a literature review, articulating theoretical frameworks, writing purpose statements, formulating research questions or hypotheses, and developing appropriate research methodologies aligned with qualitative, quantitative, or mixed methods designs.

Through hands-on writing activities, students apply critical thinking to construct the key elements of both quantitative and qualitative research proposals. Generative AI tools (e.g., ChatGPT, Google NotebookLM) are integrated to enhance writing quality and streamline research processes, with strong emphasis on ethical and responsible use. The course also nurtures a positive research attitude by fostering integrity, transparency, and accountability in anticipating and addressing ethical issues throughout the research process.

ELT301.description:
The course helps to build and develop the translation skills for 3rd year students so that at the end of the course learners will be well-versed in the English-Vietnamese and Vietnamese-English translation. 

Students are expected to acquire and apply basic knowledge of theoretical aspects covering from translation methods, translating process, equivalence, and cultural issues... in their translation.

By applying the basic theoretical knowledge, students are expected to be able to efficiently handle compiled jobs in a classroom hypothetical environment, maintain and develop basic English language skills in accordance with translation of 4 main types of texts (C1 standard) including: narrative texts,descriptiom texts, discussion texts, and dialogues.

clos.details: Demonstrate knowledge of, and ability to select, appropriate research methods for an undergraduate-level thesis.
Apply a range of digital technology tools to facilitate research processes and enhance writing quality effectively, critically, and responsibly.
Adhere to key principles of reseach ethics, such as beneficience, integrity, and respect of intellectual property, at every stage of the research process.
Present scientific research procedures, findings, and analyses clearly, rigorously, and fluently in both written and verbal formats.
Develop autonomy and accountability in completing individual tasks and meeting research deadlines.
Demonstrate strong interpersonal communication and effective collaborative working skills.
Reference source materials thoroughly and accurately, and formatted to relevant international standards.

ELT492.description:
Based on the study results of English language and specialized subjects in the previous semesters, students shall complete a Graduation thesis with the content and format appropriate to the research area to meet all course requirements. Thus, students are equipped with the knowledge and skills in scientific research and are able to present a research paper in English.

For each student, the Graduation thesis is the capstone project of their undergraduate program. Through the Graduation thesis, students are equipped with the skills of finding a topic and persistently surveying, researching, and pursuing that topic, as well as practicing writing skills to present their arguments in a logical way. Thus, they can pursue self-learning even after graduation and nurture the capability for expressing their own thoughts and ideas.

The Graduation thesis is conducted in GROUPS including 04 students (in case the students cannot be divided evenly, there can be a group of 3 or 5 students)

The instruction on the Graduation thesis is organized in two ways: in-class and in separate groups. The in-class instruction is conducted in the first week with the content regarding the rules, regulations, and things to be noticed during the process of writing the Graduation thesis. From week 2 onwards, the groups shall meet with the Thesis supervisor separately to discuss more in-depth about the group's topic.

The discussion with the Thesis supervisor can take place in many different forms appropriate to the availability of the supervisor and the students (meeting in class, online discussion, and email etc.). 

Thesis topic: the students can choose their topic in one of the following directions:
(1) Specialized English
(2) English in IT
(3) English in Economics and Trade
(4) Issues in applied linguistics
(5) Issues in English language teaching and learning
ELT492.studentTasks:
# Form groups, select and decide on a topic
# Plan and divide the workload between the members of the group
# Report the work completed on Google Form shared with group members and teacher
# Attend all in-class sessions and private group meetings with the supervisor
# Conduct, survey, and write the thesis based on the requirements of the thesis and the instructions of the supervisor
# Submit the reports, thesis, and presentation slides by the deadline
# Defend the thesis before a Graduation Thesis Council
Students are required to attend at least 80% of scheduled meetings with their supervisor(s) to be eligible for the thesis or capstone defense.

# Search engines & online databases (e.g. Google Scholar; Semantic Scholar; ResearchGate, etc.) 
# Specific research-oriented AI tools (e.g. ChatGPT Deep Research; NotebookLM; Research Rabbit; SciSpace, etc.)
# Writing and grammar check tools (e.g. Grammarly; Quillbot, etc.)
# Data collection and analysis tools (Google Forms, SPSS, Excel, etc.) 
# Plagiarism checkers (e.g. Turnitin) 
# Reference Managers (e.g. Zotero; Mendeley, etc.)
# APA Style Guide (https://apastyle.apa.org/style-grammar-guidelines/references/examples)

Students will explore topics such as radiation, waveguides, antennas, electromagnetic energy flow, and field interactions with matter. Through conceptual explanations and applied exercises, learners develop the ability to analyze, model, and interpret real-world electromagnetic phenomena used in modern technologies including communication systems, high-frequency circuits, and advanced materials.

EMP301.description:
Objectives: The goal of this course is to assist students in methodically learning the fundamentals of morphology including morphemes, allomorphs, and morphological processes. The course equips the students with the knowledge and skills to analyze word structures. After the course, students will apply key theoretical frameworks of morphology (such as Lexical Morphology, Distributed Morphology) to analyze linguistic data. They also explore how morphological processes interact with syntax, focusing on word formation and sentence structure. 

Description:
This course provides a comprehensive overview of the fundamentals of morphology and its crucial role in the study of linguistics. Students will explore the functions of words, dictionaries, and the mental lexicon in morphological analysis, gaining insight into familiar processes of lexeme formation, such as derivation and compounding, and understanding how new words are created. Furthermore, it addresses the fundamental relationship between morphology and syntax, illustrating how morphological processes can influence phonological forms. Lastly, students will engage with the basic concepts of different morphological theories, enriching their understanding of the field.

Teaching and Learning Methodology
This course employs an interactive and communicative approach, fostering engaging discussions that enhance understanding of morphology. It incorporates comprehensive guidelines for pre- and post-lesson activities, allowing students to apply and reinforce the skills they have learned. Additionally, the course supports the expansion of knowledge in related fields such as philosophy and applied meaning analysis. A receptive attitude towards questions and potential miscommunications is encouraged, creating an inclusive environment that promotes active learning and collaboration. Finally, linguistic data analysis is used for morphological analysis across specific languages.

ENB301.description:
Objectives:
The course is designed to help undergraduate students enhance their business communication via authentic and various written forms such as emails, cover letters, and CVs. With practical tips and detailed guidelines, students will be able to write more effectively and appropriately in business contexts, assuring success in delivering key messages.

Description
ENB101 addresses a wide-ranging spectrum of business communication with the straightforward seven-step method. These easy-to-follow steps save students time from start to finish, and helpful checklists will boost their confidence in business writing. Students will learn to promote themselves and their ideas clearly and concisely―whether putting together a persuasive project proposal or dealing with daily email. The course also provides comprehensive examples for all the most popular forms of communication, including slide presentations, résumés, cover letters, web copy, and a thorough guide to the art of crafting e-mails and instant messages. Insightful sidebars from experts in various fields demystify the skills of self-editing, creating content, and overcoming writer’s block, and the author’s reference-ready resources on style, punctuation, and grammar will keep students' writing error-free.

Teaching Methods:
The teaching & learning process includes a variety of methods:
From teachers’ side: lectures, guided learning, feedback and corrections; From students’ side: discussions, reading, research, writing and self-study.

Assessment scheme:
1) On-going assessment 
- Assignment 01*20% 20%
- Progress Tests 02*20% 40%
2) Final Examination: 01*40% 40%

ENG301.description: This course is designed to review and build upon students’ grammatical command of English structures in order to enhance their written and spoken performances in academic settings. The course seeks to achieve this goal in a manner that differs from typical foundational grammar courses, in that this course does not examine grammatical features in isolation from one another (e.g., spending a week on the past tense without looking at other tenses); instead, this class examines grammar points as smaller systems lodged within a larger system (e.g., examining all verb tenses together to understand how they function as a group). Students will practice covered structures, and will produce several original works that will grammatically evolve over the course of the quarter (as more and more material is covered).

ENM111.description:
This course is designed to improve learner's business English skills, confidence and fluency in using the English language within various situations and context. Upon completion of the course, students should be able to:
* understand different business concepts and re-affirm grammar rules at the beginner’s level and extend their business vocabulary; 
 * develop listening skills and enhance their comprehension of gist and listening for detailed information skills. 
* improve their speaking skills and discuss business topic and concepts with confidence and apply wider communication skills in a variety of business situations and contexts.
* enrich their reading skills involving informative, stimulating, and up-to-date business-related texts. 
* develop writing skills, with specific focus on writing short e-mails. 
Skills development
Students will be assisted in developing their skills in reading, writing, listening and speaking through business English syllabus with exercises exploring:
* skimming, 
* scanning, 
* detailed reading, 
* guessing unknown words from context, 
* understanding text organization, 
*recognizing argument and counter-argument; 
* distinguishing between main information and supporting detail, fact and opinion, hypothesis versus evidence;
* summarising and note-taking.
Writing skills will encompass:
* Essay content and structure (patterns of organization, paragraphing, discussion – developing balanced argument and counter-argument, exposing advantages and disadvantages of issues discussed with original ideas in a coherent and cohesive manner with correct punctuation). 
* Functions (generalization, definitions, exemplification, classification, comparison and contrast, cause and effect, process and procedure, interpretation of data). 
* Style (avoiding passive constructions and verbosity). 
Listening skills will include:
* conversations between several businesspeople in a variety of business situations requiring students to listen for gist and detailed information and evaluate the importance of information. 
* supplementary fun and stimulating audio-visual files exploring grammar and English in social situations. 
Speaking skills will include:
* developing effective business communication skills through debating, pitching for a point, agreeing and disagreeing, clarifying, questioning and concluding. 
* Understanding and using simple presentation skills encompassing introductions, stating a purpose, signposting, highlighting key points of a paragraph, summarizing and developing convincing and logical conclusions. 
* listening to and comprehending equivalent to IELTS score 4.5-5.0);
* speaking to peers and lecturers (within the framework of Breakthrough level-A1).

assessments.questionType: Teachers can flexibly choose different formats for students to complete the assignment. Here are some suggestions for teachers to choose:Suggestion 1: Students record speakers who have mispronunciations (they can be students from outside the class or students within the class) and use those recordings as the main material for creating the pronunciation guide. Those short clips should only be used as practice examples or for comparison with the mispronounced samples. The content should focus only on analyzing consonant and vowel sounds.Students analyze the clip focusing only on the content they have learned:A. Consonant Sounds· Identify and list examples of consonants in the clip that are commonly difficult for Vietnamese learners (e.g., /θ/, /ð/, /ʃ/, /tʃ/, /ʒ/, /v/, /z/, final stops /p t k/, etc.).· Provide short IPA transcriptions only for word-level items, not full sentences.· Identify misleading spellings (e.g., “knife” /naɪf/)B. Vowel Sounds· Identify key vowel sounds in the clip that differ significantly from Vietnamese vowels.· Provide minimal IPA transcription of sample words (e.g., ship vs sheep, cup vs calf).· Comment briefly on vowel length contrasts or tense vs. lax vowel differences, if applicable.No analysis of diphthongs, triphthongs, stress, linking, rhythm, or intonation.Group Collaboration:Work in teams of 3–4 to compile findings and present them in a short video or slide presentation.Suggestion 2:Students work in pairs and make a dialogue in which they should use the following aspects of sounds (the same as Speaking part 1 in FE)- Vowels- Consonants- Dipthongs- Elision- Linking consonant sounds to vowel sounds- Intrusion- Assimilation

clos.details: Recognize and accurately produce consonant sounds of English, and differentiate them clearly in both spoken and written (IPA) forms, with support from AI pronunciation feedback tools.
Recognize and accurately produce vowel sounds of English, and distinguish vowel contrasts through listening and transcription tasks supported by AI analysis.
Recognize and accurately produce diphthongs and triphthongs of English, and demonstrate clear differences between similar complex vowels using AI-assisted pronunciation practice.
Demonstrate fluency and appropriate prosody—intonation patterns, sentence stress—to express different meanings and emotions in spoken English, using AI models for practice and comparison.
Apply rules of connected speech (linking, assimilation, elision, weak forms) to produce smoother and more natural speech, with reinforcement from AI-based listening and speaking tools.

Collaborate effectively in pairs and groups to practice pronunciation, solve phonetic/phonological tasks, provide peer feedback, and engage in sustained pronunciation improvement supported by AI-enhanced learning resources.

ENP102.description:
Objectives: Help students develop clear and intelligible English pronunciation with a neutral and comprehensible accent.
 Help students recognize and produce individual English consonant sounds, including place of articulation, manner of articulation, voicing contrasts, aspiration, difficult contrasts (/θ/–/s/, /ʃ/–/s/, /r/–/l/…) (e.g., /θ/–/s/, /ʃ/–/s/, /r/–/l/)
 Help students identify diversity of sound systems.
 Help students know how to use AI-assisted tools to practice pronunciation tools (e.g., ELSA, SpeechAce, Speechling) to receive instant feedback, identify mispronounced sounds, and improve segmental features.
 Help students know how to recognize and produce correct word stress, sentence stress, weak forms, linking, and rhythm.
 Help students know how to practice shadowing with AI-generated audio to improve naturalness and speech fluency.
 Help students know how to distinguish segmental features
 Help students know how to diagnose personal listening weaknesses through AI performance analytics.
 Help students know how to develop self-learning habits using AI apps for daily pronunciation practice.
'-Description: 'This course covers key features of English pronunciation, including consonants, vowels, diphthongs, sound combinations, word and sentence stress, rhythm, intonation, tone, accents, and phonemic symbols. '-Teaching method: optional
'- Apply AI tools effectively to support self-study, self-practice.

- IPA Transcriber AI – tự động chuyển văn bản sang phiên âm IPA

- ChatGPT – tạo bài tập nhận diện âm, minimal pairs, stress patterns
- Twee – tạo bài trắc nghiệm minimal pairs, word stress
- Quizizz AI – tạo quiz nghe–chọn âm, phân biệt âm dễ nhầm
- Edpuzzle AI – tạo bài nghe dựa trên video phát â
- Genially AI – làm bài tập kéo–thả IPA hoặc matching

- VocalImage / AnatomyNext – mô phỏng 3D articulators
- Wakaru / SoundLab AI – hình ảnh hóa sóng âm, formant, spectrogram
- Canva AI – tạo infographic về vowel chart / consonant chart
- Descript – tạo audio waveform và chỉnh sửa giọng bằng AI

assessments.questionType: Teachers can flexibly choose different formats for students to complete the assignment. Here are some suggestions for teachers to choose:Suggestion 1: Students record speakers who have mispronunciations (they can be students from outside the class or students within the class) and use those recordings as the main material for creating the pronunciation guide. Those short clips should only be used as practice examples or for comparison with the mispronounced samples. The content should focus only on analyzing consonant and vowel sounds.Students analyze the clip focusing only on the content they have learned:A. Consonant Sounds· Identify and list examples of consonants in the clip that are commonly difficult for Vietnamese learners (e.g., /θ/, /ð/, /ʃ/, /tʃ/, /ʒ/, /v/, /z/, final stops /p t k/, etc.).· Provide short IPA transcriptions only for word-level items, not full sentences.· Identify misleading spellings (e.g., “knife” /naɪf/)B. Vowel Sounds· Identify key vowel sounds in the clip that differ significantly from Vietnamese vowels.· Provide minimal IPA transcription of sample words (e.g., ship vs sheep, cup vs calf).· Comment briefly on vowel length contrasts or tense vs. lax vowel differences, if applicable.No analysis of diphthongs, triphthongs, stress, linking, rhythm, or intonation.Group Collaboration:Work in teams of 3–4 to compile findings and present them in a short video or slide presentation.Suggestion 2:Students work in pairs and make a dialogue in which they should use the following aspects of sounds (the same as Speaking part 1 in FE)- Vowels- Consonants- Dipthongs- Elision- Linking consonant sounds to vowel sounds- Intrusion- Assimilation

ENR501.description:
Inside Reading 4 combines reading skills development with key vocabulary from the Academic Word List, to give students the tools they need to understand academic texts.

Each unit features two high interest readings. Topics include Sociology, Nutrition, Architecture, and Business, among many others. At the higher levels of Inside Reading, reading texts are adapted from authentic, well-known sources such as the Wall Street Journal, Popular Science, and The New York Times, and from acclaimed authors such as Malcolm Gladwell, James Surowiecki, and Jared Diamond. Authentic readings expose students to real-world, high interest content and authentic language.

Explicit reading skill instruction provides the foundation for effective critical reading. At all levels, Inside Reading covers reading skills that are vital to student success in the academic classroom, such as previewing and predicting, finding the main idea, scanning, and evaluating.

assessments.questionType: Description:In this assignment, students will design Course Learning Outcomes (CLOs) for an English as a Foreign Language (EFL) course. This task will require students to apply the principles of Outcome-Based Education (OBE) and understand the significance of basing education on outcomes. Students will create CLOs that reflect the essential skills and competencies students should acquire by the end of the course. Students should consider integrating the cognitive domains of learning from Bloom’s Taxonomy.Context:Imagine you are part of a team of educational consultants who have been hired by a prestigious language institute to revamp their English as a Foreign Language (EFL) program. The institute’s goal is to offer a cutting-edge course that not only enhances students' language skills but also prepares them to thrive in an increasingly globalized world. To achieve this, the institute has decided to adopt an Outcome-Based Education (OBE) approach, ensuring that every aspect of the course is aligned with clearly defined learning outcomes.Step-by-step guidelines:Identify the Course ObjectivesIdentify Key OutcomesFormulate Your CLOs Using Bloom’s Taxonomy as a GuidelineEnsure CLOs Are SMART
assessments.knowledgeAndSkill: OBE
assessments.gradingGuide: Group work (3-4 people/ a group) with a clear task delegation

The WebQuests will serve as a guide for students to complete a project based on the Course Learning Outcomes (CLOs) students have designed in the previous assignment. This WebQuests should include a clear project idea, a driving question, steps for project implementation, useful resources, and a conclusion with a feedback form.Design a webquest for a project of the course in Assignment 1 including: - the project idea and artifacts - a driving question - task and process of the project implementation (steps) - useful sources for students to work on the project - a conclusion with a feedback form- at least one AI tool during the creation of your WebQuest.

Objectives:
 The course is designed to help undergraduate students to grasp the key concepts and practices of persuasive communication today. Through real-life situations as well as authentic materials, students will be able to develop their communication and persuasion skills.

Description
 EPC301 provides students with a comprehensive yet accessible overview of the study and practice of persuasive communication. It also demonstrates how theories and research illuminate and adapt to the present digital era, with continued attention to ethical implications and today’s big topics. The course includes up-to-date definitions of key terms in the field as they relate to present-day practice; an integration of persuasion theories and the ubiquity of online influence; new examples and cases to illustrate persuasive communication’s approach to health campaigns, attitudes, communicator appeals, dissonance, and ethics; and a thorough reflection of the most current scholarship in the field.

EPG301.description:
- Course objective: The aim of the course is to enable students to critically evaluate how context impacts the interpretation of meaning in communication. Additionally, students will be equipped to apply their understanding of pragmatics in order to produce precise and contextually appropriate content in English for various communicative purposes. 

- Course description: This course focuses on how context influences the interpretation of meaning in communication. The course provides understanding on contextual meaning so that students will be able to analyze how context, including cultural background and situational factors, shapes the meaning of utterances. 1. Emphasize the practical skills that students will learn in this course. 2. Observe coherence and consistency in using active voice statements. 3. The course includes an exploration of speech act concepts, illustrating how utterances can serve as requests, commands, questions, or statements based on the context in which they are used.
Concepts of speech acts, including how utterances can function as requests, commands, questions, or statements, depending on context are provided with . Mastery of pragmatics equips students with the ability to navigate complex social and professional situations, fostering better negotiation, collaboration, and overall communication competence, which are invaluable assets in careers such as business, education, law, media, and international relations. 

- Teaching and Learning Methodology: This course applies instructional, communicative, and interactive discussions. Instructions on pre-lesson and post lesson exercises are designed to apply learnt skills. Open minded approach to questions and any misunderstandings that may arise during lessons is preferred. Group work and pair work are encouraged to foster interaction and discussion. Group presentations are carried out to reflect students' comprehension on pragmatic aspects in the course. Linguistic data analysis may particularly be included as the students are required to do the Assignment across specific languages.

ESL101.description:
Objectives:
This course is designed to introduce students to the basic concepts of Sociolinguistics and the relationship between language and society, and how language is used in multilingual speech communities. 
Description:
The course helps students:
~Understand sociolinguistic terminology or concepts to apply in research and real-life practices. 
~Use language appropriately in different social contexts.
~Interpret the social relationships in a community, and the way people convey and construct aspects of their social identity through language.
~Examine some similarities and differences in the way people use their language to convey meaning in association with society.
Teaching method:
This course applies instructional, communicative, and interactive discussions with:
~instructions on lessons and exercises meant to apply learnt skills.
~researching features of sociolinguistics through presentations and project work.
~open-minded approach to questions and issues that may arise during lessons.
~lectures and seminars to enhance interest in the field of sociolinguistics.

ESP301m.description:
This course is based on the "An Introduction to Programming the Internet of Things (IoT)" Specialization at https://www.coursera.org/specializations/iot. 
The course covers embedded systems, the Raspberry Pi Platform and the Arduino environment for building devices that can control the physical world. Unlike traditional computer-based systems, IoT devices are “embedded” within other devices in order to provide enhanced functionality without exposing the user to the complexities of a computer. In terms of programming, Arduino - an open-source computer hardware/software platform for building digital devices and interactive objects, is a great choice for controlling small devices, whereas the Raspberry Pi - a small single-board computer, is useful for designing and developing practical IoT devices.
Students must complete the IOT102 course before participating in this course. Students will start with a detailed introduction to the internet of things and embedded systems, then work with Arduino and program in C, then work with Raspberry Pi and program in Python, and finally produce a group project. In this final project, students will apply the skills learned by designing, building and testing a microcontroller-based embedded system, completing a unique final project that can be listed as an achievement in their CVs.

EST301.description:
Course description: 
This course offers an introduction to the practical analysis of English sentence structure and is designed for English learners who are into the field of linguistics.The course provides key concepts in English sentence structure such as constituency, category and functions, employing tree diagrams and practices of drawing tree diagrams which help learners make sense of the knowledge provided. The exercises are relevant, not only for reviewing syntactic aspects and discussions of in-text exercises but also for constructing interrelationships between syntactic knowledge in different languages and ones of related areas in linguistics. References for further reading are given at the end of each chapter to offer learners choices for extensive reading about related subjects. 
Course objective: 
The course aims to provide students knowledge of syntax for applying to their studying linguistics and for generating accurate content in English for different communication purposes. 
Teaching and Learning Methodology: 
This course applies instructional, communicative, and interactive discussions. It is appropriate for different teaching and learning tendencies involving instructors' instructions on pre-lesson and post lesson exercises meant to apply learnt skills; ancillary lectures and seminars to enhance active interest in the topics; or interactive discussions leading by students followed by instructors' feedback and conclusions. Open-mindedness and questions from both students and instructors are encouraged if misunderstandings related to the subject knowledge arise.

ETM101.description:
Teaching Methodology is aimed to help teachers-to-be develop practical skills in teaching English as a foreign language. It concentrates on methods and techniques which do not require lengthy preparation of material, elaborate use of aids or equipment, or complex forms of classroom organization. The course is also designed to encourage an active style of teacher training with teachers-to-be participating as fully as possible. Using the course on a training session will involve three main kinds of activity: demonstration, discussion, and pair/group work. 
This course is designed to provide a systematic introduction to and a thorough instructions on effective teaching methodology.
Upon completion of the course, students should be able to:

LO1. *Understand the basics of teaching and the roles of teachers; *understand the nature of student-centered classrooms; *understand the essence of individual, pair and group work; *handle basic teaching situations inside classroom; *identify the 3-stage process of a teaching session.
LO2. *Identify the stages of teaching vocabulary; *conduct vocabulary teaching appropriately and effectively.

Design and generate pedagogically sound ESL/EFL lesson ideas through the effective use of AI 
and digital learning tools, ensuring alignment with specified lesson outcomes and curriculum standards.

Implement AI-supported instructional strategies that respond to learners’ linguistic 
backgrounds, individual needs, and affective factors such as motivation and language anxiety.

Critically evaluate the effectiveness of ESL/EFL lesson demonstrations by utilizing AI-assisted 
observation and reflection tools to identify pedagogical strengths and areas for enhancement.
Justify, through evidence-based reasoning, the influence of teacher behaviour and AI-supported classroom interactions on learners’ motivation and engagement.

Apply AI-driven assessment and feedback systems to monitor, analyse, and improve learner 
performance and language development in ESL/EFL contexts.

Demonstrate ethical awareness and professional responsibility in the use of AI technologies for 
language teaching, ensuring fairness, data privacy, and inclusivity in learning environments.

clos.details: Identify and explain the fundamental concepts, types, and roles of planned events in contemporary society.
Analyze the event planning process and apply tools for scheduling, risk management, budgeting, and evaluation.
Critically evaluate the social, cultural, economic, and environmental impacts of planned events.
Design and present a comprehensive event proposal that integrates creativity, communication strategy, stakeholder coordination, and technical elements.
Demonstrate teamwork, problem-solving, and creativity in the development and presentation of event-related projects.

EVN205.description: This course provides an in-depth exploration of event studies, with a specific focus on the theory and practice of planned events. It critically examines the multifaceted roles events play within socio-cultural, economic, political, and environmental contexts. Through a blend of conceptual frameworks and international case studies, students will analyze diverse event typologies—ranging from local festivals to global mega-events—while assessing their strategic significance and broader impacts. Emphasis is placed on equipping students with essential competencies in event planning, stakeholder management, risk mitigation, and outcome evaluation. In addition, the course investigates the application of event strategies in media, public relations, and brand activation, encompassing formats such as product launches, press events, trade exhibitions, and live entertainment. Contemporary practices in sponsorship negotiation, collaborative event design, crisis communication, and the integration of emerging technologies—including AI and digital platforms—are also addressed, preparing students for effective and innovative event delivery in dynamic real-world settings.

EVN301.description: This course provides a comprehensive overview of the events industry, equipping students with the knowledge and skills required to plan and execute successful events. Students will explore the key characteristics of events, examine the role of industry bodies, and analyze the events business as a service industry. The course delves into the scope and impact of events on society, the economy, and politics, while offering a thorough understanding of event planning processes, including budgeting, marketing, and logistics. It places strong emphasis on strategic event management, project management techniques, and risk management strategies. A highlight of the course is the opportunity for hands-on experience through a real-world project, where students will apply their learning to organize a complete event.

clos.details:
Understand the concept of FPGA, its key features, and its role in engineering applications.
Differentiate between other hardware tools such as Microcontrollers, ASICs, and FPGA. Evaluate and select the appropriate tool for each design scenario. Analyze system requirements to decide whether to use FPGA or another solution.

Understand how the Look-Up Table (LUT) operates in FPGA, including performing Boolean algebra and replacing dedicated logic gates in hardware design: the role and working principle of LUTs in FPGA, learn how LUTs perform Boolean algebra to handle logical operations, analyze and design logic systems using LUTs instead of traditional logic gates, apply LUTs to optimize hardware designs.

Understand how Flip-Flops, a fundamental component of FPGA, operate, including storing state to provide the device with memory of previous events: the role and working principle of Flip-Flops in FPGA, learn how Flip-Flops store state to create internal memory within FPGA, design and implement logic systems using Flip-Flops to store states, analyze how Flip-Flops manage states in sequential circuit designs.

Learn how to write testbenches to simulate FPGA designs, verify code functionality, identify bugs, and understand abnormal behaviors in the system: the role of testbenches in simulating and testing FPGA designs, how simulations can be used to investigate code behavior and detect errors, write testbenches to test and simulate the functionality of FPGA designs, analyze simulation results to identify bugs and improve designs.

Learn how to create basic building blocks common to FPGA designs, including multiplexers, demultiplexers, shift registers, FIFO, and other memory structures, as well as how to combine them to solve complex problems: the working principles of common modules, how to use and combine these building blocks in FPGA designs, design and implement basic building blocks in FPGA to address real-world problems, integrate FPGA modules to create solutions for complex issues.

How to expand the FPGA build process, including details about synthesis, the place and route stage, recognizing timing errors, how to avoid them, and how to safely cross between clock domains within FPGA designs: the synthesis and place-and-route process in FPGA design, timing errors and how to prevent, analyze and resolve timing errors in FPGA designs, safe transitions between clock domains to ensure system reliability.

How to use the state machine, a common model for tracking logical flow through a sequence of events in FPGA: the concept and operational principles of state machines, use state machines to manage logical flow in FPGA designs, design and implement state machines and create interactive applications

How to utilize essential FPGA components beyond LUT and flip-flop: understand the functions and roles such as block RAM, DSP block, and PLL, apply strategies to effectively utilize FPGA components in design, develop solutions that optimize FPGA resources to meet system requirements.

How to work with numbers and implement mathematical operations in FPGA: the differences between signed and unsigned numbers, fixed-point numbers, floating-point numbers, apply mathematical operations to solve technical problems, design and implement algorithms using signed, unsigned, fixed-point, and floating-point numbers.

Learn to explore the input/output (I/O) capabilities: understand the I/O capabilities and function, the pros and cons of various types of I/O interfaces, apply knowledge of different I/O interfaces to design systems compatible with FPGA.

FAP201.description:
- Introduction to FPGA, comparison of FPGA with other technologies such as microcontrollers and ASICs, FPGA programming languages: Verilog and VHDL, and common applications of FPGA.
- Approach models and terms such as: entity, architecture, process statements, behavioral modeling, sequential processing, parallel processing...
- Explore and utilize FPGA programming instructions: libraries, entity descriptions, architecture descriptions, data objects, data types, data conversion, operators, data attributes, signal attributes, subprograms and packages, sequential processing instructions, parallel processing instructions...
- Use hardware and software tools to execute the design process: testing (testbench), synthesis, place and route, run simulation, waveform analysis, debugging...
- Execute design projects such as: combinational logic circuits, flip-flop, counters, registers, shifters, shift registers, encoding and decoding, demultiplexers and multiplexers, memory, state machine, communication...

FGU301.description:
This comprehensive Basic Unity Training Program is designed to equip participants with essential skills in Unity game development, empowering them to create engaging and interactive 2D and 3D games. Building upon strong foundation in C# programming, the course delves into advanced topics such as 3D game development, physics, animations, and user interface design. Through a combination of theoretical lectures, hands-on labs, and collaborative projects, participants will gain practical experience and confidence in using Unity to bring their game ideas to life.

Key Learning Outcomes:
- Master C# Programming: Gain a deep understanding of C# syntax, data structures, algorithms, and object-oriented programming principles.
- Navigate the Unity Environment: Become proficient in using Unity's interface and tools for game development.
- Develop 3D Games: Learn the fundamentals of 3D game development, including rendering, lighting, animations, and physics.
- Create Engaging Game Worlds: Master the art of designing game objects, animations, and physics components to create immersive and interactive game environments.
- Build User-Friendly Interfaces: Design intuitive and visually appealing user interfaces that enhance the player experience.
- Develop Games from Start to Finish: Complete hands-on projects, applying your knowledge to create your own small games and interactive applications.
- Collaborate Effectively: Work collaboratively with teammates to develop game projects, fostering effective communication and teamwork skills.

FIN201.description: The course is an intermediate-level course in macroeconomics, including topics in international, monetary, and financial economics. The goal of the course is to provide a coherent framework for analyzing macroeconomic events, such as business cycles (recessions and booms) and long-run growth, their impact on financial markets, and to discuss macroeconomic policy. Finishing this course, students will be well-versed in macroeconomic and finance areas, be able to realize the implications of real-life macroeconomic policy/ events on the global financial markets.

FIN304.description:

framing effects, will be examined. It then can compare and contrast rational and behavioral theories of finance and financial decision making. This extends students’ knowledge of finance
by demonstrating how “real” investors and markets do not always correspond to the rational agents and outcomes described in standard finance courses.

assessments.gradingGuide: - Guided by instructor - Example of group assignment: Acquisition Team Project: Early in the term students will divide into “teams” of four-to-six students each to share the research, analysis, and field work required to design a viable corporate acquisition proposal. The purpose of the Acquisition Project is to give students the opportunity to apply the tools they have learned in an increasingly common situation, i.e., mergers and acquisitions. Each team will be asked to represent an acquiring company or investment group whose business strategy involves an acquisition or merger. The acquiring and target firms must be in the same industry. The acquisition can involve a recent transaction (i.e., last 12 to 18 months), a current transaction, or a hypothetical transaction involving two publicly traded firms, private companies, or some combination. The use of publicly traded companies will facilitate data collection, and the selection of companies in the same industry will simplify the analysis by eliminating the need to analyze two different industries. Selecting Companies to Study: The success of the Project will be greatly dependent on the Team’s ability to understand the company’s operations, products, and the competitive dynamics of the industry in which it competes and to obtain financial, technical and market-related information on the company. Teams are encouraged (but not required) to select a publicly traded company, because both internal financial and operating data, as well as market/industry data, is likely to be more readily available (e.g., through Disclosure, Value Line, Standard & Poors Corporate Register, Thomas Register, etc.) than for a privately owned firm.

FTM301.description:

- Comprehend the evolving relationship between financial technology (FinTech) and managerial applications, analyzing how technological advancements reshape financial decision-making and business strategies.
- Identify key challenges and opportunities that traditional financial institutions and businesses face in adapting to fintech innovations.
- Evaluate the role of fintech solutions in enhancing operational efficiency, reducing costs, and driving strategic decision-making in financial management.
- Apply insights from The FINTECH Book to real-world business scenarios, assessing the implications of financial disintermediation and digital transformation.
2. Course Content: Regulatory frameworks and challenges for financial institutions; the emergence and impact of fintech disruptors; technological innovation in financial services; financial disintermediation and its broader economic implications. 
3. Activities and Teaching Methodology: The course combines engaging lectures, real-world case studies on fintech innovations, interactive group discussions, and hands-on projects that analyze the transformative impact of technology on financial systems.

clos.details: Identify relevant generative-AI techniques (LLMs, diffusion, multimodal, RAG, agents, fine-tuning, alignment) for a capstone topic.
Formulate problem statements, scope, objectives, and success criteria in a project proposal.
Plan data preparation, model selection, and licensing/ethics review.
Conduct baseline analysis using pre-trained models, prompting, and in-context learning.
Develop and adapt generative-AI systems to project requirements.
Evaluate and optimize systems using appropriate metrics and protocols, with attention to contamination and saturation.
Interpret outputs and failure modes (hallucination, bias, jailbreak) and visualize results for stakeholders.
Summarize conclusions and actionable recommendations, including deployment and cost/latency trade-offs.
Compile a final report with an explicit ethics, safety, and provenance subsection.
Deliver oral presentations with live demonstrations and Q&A defense.

GAP301.description:
This capstone project course is designed to consolidate and apply students' knowledge in generative AI and large language models through a substantial team project. Students scope, design, build, evaluate, and present a non-trivial generative AI system or empirical study. Topics applied include:
- The application of generative AI techniques (LLMs, diffusion, RAG, agents, fine-tuning) to solve practical problems.
- The identification and adaptation of generative AI methodologies from current research for specific use cases.
- The development of a comprehensive solution approach using prompt engineering, retrieval-augmented generation, fine-tuning (LoRA / QLoRA), or agent design.
- The evaluation and analysis of generative outputs using appropriate metrics (perplexity, ROUGE, faithfulness, FID, human / LLM-as-judge protocols) and rigorous failure-mode analysis.
- Recognition of appropriate scenarios for prompting vs RAG vs fine-tuning vs agent design.
- Selection of suitable metrics and benchmarks for generative-system evaluation.
- Understanding the ethical, safety, provenance, and legal implications of generative AI (hallucination, bias, deepfakes, copyright, content provenance / C2PA).
- Implementation and reflection on generative pipelines including data preparation, model adaptation, inference / serving, and post-deployment monitoring.
- Effective teamwork and project management across a multi-phase delivery.
GAP301.studentTasks:
- Select a suitable generative AI project and form teams (2-3 members).
- Allocate and schedule tasks among team members.
- Develop a project output that meets the specified requirements and demonstrates individual contribution.
- Submit four progressive reports (Proposal; Data & Baseline; Model & Results; Final Project Report) on time per the schedule.
- Disclose any use of AI tools as required by each report, and be able to explain and defend all submitted work and code.
- Present and defend the project in front of a review panel at the final oral examination.
- Promptly access the FU FLM at https://flm.fpt.edu.vn/ for up-to-date course information.
GAP301.tools:
- Programming Languages: Python 3.10+
- Software Tools: Jupyter Notebook / Google Colab, PyTorch, Hugging Face Transformers, Diffusers, PEFT, TRL, LangChain, vLLM
- Models: Hosted frontier APIs (Claude, GPT, Gemini) and open-weight families (Llama, Mistral, Qwen, DeepSeek)
- Datasets: Hugging Face Datasets, Kaggle, publicly licensed corpora
- Additional Resources: Papers with Code, arXiv, GitHub, Hugging Face Hub, Weights & Biases for experiment tracking
GAP301.note:
- The essential capstone project is mandatory, focusing on solving a real-world generative-AI problem. It consists of four progressive reports and a final oral presentation.
- The final mark is determined by summing the weighted scores of: Report 1 - Project Proposal (10%), Report 2 - Data & Baseline (20%), Report 3 - Model & Results (30%), Report 4 - Final Project Report (10%), and Final Exam - Oral group presentation (30%).
- The final exam (oral group presentation) takes place in class, individually evaluated by one professor / lecturer or a review panel.
- Completion Criteria: every assessment component > 0 AND Final Exam Score >= 4 AND Final Result >= 5.

GLA301.description:
Air Cargo Management is a practice‑oriented course that equips you with the knowledge and skills to manage the full life cycle of air freight operations. It focuses on how airlines, freight forwarders, ground handlers, and shippers work together to move high‑value cargo safely, quickly, and profitably in today’s global supply chains.

Across 11 chapters you will explore industry structure and regulations, the role of IATA cargo agents and forwarders, aircraft and ULD characteristics, airport and terminal facilities, cargo handling processes, booking and acceptance procedures, and the management of special cargo such as perishables and dangerous goods. You will also learn how to calculate air cargo rates and charges, complete and interpret airway bills, and understand the growing importance of cargo digitalization and automation.

Throughout the course, real cases and examples will illustrate how air cargo supports trade and logistics development in Vietnam, helping you see clear links between theory and local industry practice. By the end of the module, you will be able to design and evaluate air cargo solutions, communicate effectively with international partners, and position yourself for careers with airlines, 3PLs, e‑commerce logistics providers, and airport operators.

GLC301.method: - Offline.- Research-Based Learning (RBL) integration:Selected topics in this course are delivered using a lResearch-Based Learning (RBL) approach. Rather than converting the entire course into a full research-based subject, the course integrates one focused RBL mini-module in Unit 6 (E-Customs Procedures and Documentation), where students investigate declaration errors and documentary inconsistencies, analyze evidence, propose corrective actions, defend their decisions, and reflect on compliance implications. This design supports inquiry-driven learning, evidence-based reasoning, academic defence, and reflective practice while remaining feasible for a technical, application-oriented course in Semester 5.

clos.details: Explain the role of customs administration, trade compliance, and the legal-institutional framework governing e-customs operations in Vietnam within the context of global logistics and supply chain management.
Apply HS classification principles to determine appropriate tariff headings for typical traded goods and justify classification decisions using product information and legal notes.
Apply customs valuation, origin-related preferential treatment, tariff rules, and tax principles to determine customs value and payable import taxes in common customs scenarios.
Prepare and review the logic, data fields, supporting documents, and procedural steps of electronic customs declarations for standard import/export and selected special customs regimes.

GLC301.description:
This course provides specialized and applied knowledge of electronic customs declaration and customs compliance in global logistics and supply chain operations. It equips students with the legal, technical, and procedural foundations required to understand customs administration; apply HS classification (Harmonized System Codes Classification), customs valuation, origin-related preferential treatment, and tariff/tax rules; and prepare and review e-customs declaration logic, supporting documents, and declaration flows for standard import/export and selected customs regimes. Through scenario-based learning, guided discussion, document review, and case analysis grounded in FIATA (International Federation of Freight Forwarders Associations) and VLI (Vietnam Logistics Research and Development Institute) resources, students develop compliance awareness, professional responsibility, and practical decision-making skills relevant to customs, freight forwarding, and international logistics environments.

clos.details: Explain the fundamental concepts of goods and insurance in commercial, transport, and logistics activities, including the characteristics, classification, packaging, marking, storage, and risk exposure of goods.
Identify and classify different types of goods, especially dangerous goods, based on their characteristics, hazardous properties, and relevant transport requirements in logistics operations.

Apply international regulations and standard procedures related to the transport of goods, including the classification, packing, marking, labelling, and documentation requirements for dangerous goods shipments.

Analyze the roles, responsibilities, and training requirements of the parties involved in the transport and transit chain in order to ensure compliance and safety in goods handling and transportation.

Apply the principal concepts of cargo insurance, including insurable interest, indemnity, subrogation, marine risks, and types of losses, to assess risk exposure and determine suitable insurance protection for different categories of goods.

Evaluate cargo loss or damage situations and perform appropriate actions, including selecting suitable insurance cover under Institute Cargo Clauses (A), (B), and (C), preparing transport documentation, and handling insurance claims effectively.

GLH301.description: Goods and Insurance is a course that introduces fundamental knowledge about goods in commercial, transportation, and logistics activities, while also highlighting the role of insurance in protecting goods against risks arising during storage, handling, and transportation. The course focuses on topics such as the characteristics and classification of goods, requirements for packaging, labeling, and storage, common risks associated with goods, basic principles of insurance, cargo insurance conditions, and the claims process in case of loss or damage. Through this course, learners can understand the relationship between the nature of different types of goods and their corresponding risk levels, thereby enabling them to select appropriate insurance methods to minimize losses, support risk management, and enhance efficiency in logistics and international trade operations.

GLI201.description: This course equips students with foundational and practical knowledge of international trade, viewed through the lens of supply chain and logistics management. It explores the roles of key stakeholders in global trade, the interplay between international trade and freight forwarding, and the structure of trade contracts. Students will examine critical elements such as Incoterms 2020, delivery and payment terms, and common risks in cross-border transactions. The course also covers international trade regulations, major institutions governing global commerce, and financial and legal frameworks, including trade financing and dispute resolution mechanisms. Through hands-on case studies and the use of standard documentation, students will develop essential skills to effectively navigate global trade environments and contribute to trade operations in logistics and supply chain organizations.

materials.author: Robert A. Novack, Brian Gibson, John J. Coyle

clos.details: Identify and recall fundamental concepts of international transport management, including various transport modes, multimodal transport mode and its documents, import-export procedures and key global transport organizations.
Explain the roles and impacts of transportation in supply chain systems, including its economic, environmental, and social significance.
Demonstrate the ability to apply transport management techniques such as total cost analysis, carrier selection, and mode choice in solving real-world logistics challenges.
Analyze complex global transportation scenarios by evaluating trade-offs, regulatory frameworks, and market dynamics affecting transport decisions.
Critically assess the effectiveness of transport strategies (e.g., multimodal vs. intermodal, hub-and-spoke models) in improving supply chain performance.
Design an integrated transport management plan that optimizes routing, mode selection, and distribution networks, incorporating tools such as TMS (Transportation Management Systems).
Show professionalism, ethical behavior, and social responsibility while collaborating effectively on group projects.

GLT301.description: The course International Transport Management offers a comprehensive understanding of the essential role transportation plays in the global supply chain. Students are introduced to major modes of transportation—including ocean, air, land, rail, and multimodal systems—while analyzing their functions, costs, and operational efficiencies. Core topics include the concept of landed cost, transportation's impact on inventory and service trade-offs, derived demand, and demand elasticity. The curriculum also covers the structure of global transport corridors (transport, trade, and legal), and the strategic importance of international organizations such as IATA, FIATA, and the International Chamber of Shipping. Special attention is given to international commercial terms (Incoterms), HS codes, and trade agreements that govern cross-border logistics. Practical methods, such as the Clarke and Wright Savings Algorithm for route optimization, are explored to equip students with tools for real-world problem-solving. The course also emphasizes how Transportation Management Systems (TMS) contribute to operational efficiency. By understanding how transportation supports functions like last-mile delivery, global trade connectivity, and just-in-time inventory models, students are prepared to make strategic decisions in logistics and supply chain environments. Ultimately, this course provides both foundational knowledge and managerial insight into navigating the complexities of international transport in today’s fast-evolving marketplace.

materials.author: Joshua Glazer, Sanjay Madhav

clos.details: Understand basic networking concepts (TCP/IP model, IP addressing, DNS) and game networking history.
Differentiate between common game network architectures (Client-Server, P2P, Dedicated Server) and their use cases.
Ability to implement data serialization using Binary and JSON formats to optimize network transmission.
Ability to build RESTful APIs using .NET Core and integrate MongoDB for player data storage.
Ability to program network communication systems using TCP and Reliable UDP via the LiteNetLib library.
Understand the principles of data synchronization (RPC, State Synchronization) and authority management.
Understand industry-standard lag compensation techniques (Client-side Prediction, Interpolation, and Server Reconciliation).
Understand the process of game server deployment using Docker and fundamental security measures.

GNS301.description:
GNS301 is an intensive course designed to bridge the gap between game development and backend engineering. You will master the "hidden" infrastructure of online gaming—from raw data transmission and latency optimization to scalable server architectures. By the end of this course, you will be able to build secure, high-performance multiplayer environments capable of supporting real-time global interactions.

Key Learning Outcomes:
- Master Low-Level Networking: Build custom servers using TCP and Reliable UDP (LiteNetLib). Learn to handle raw sockets and binary serialization for maximum bandwidth efficiency.
- Combat Latency: Implement industry-standard lag-compensation techniques, including Client-side Prediction, Interpolation, and Server Reconciliation to ensure smooth gameplay.
- Architect Scalable Systems: Apply professional 3-Layer Architecture (Presentation, Logic, Data) to backend development. Integrate MongoDB for persistence and Docker for containerized deployment.

By the end of this course, you will have the skills to architect and develop a complete multiplayer ecosystem. You will possess the technical confidence to build not just a game, but a secure, scalable, and professional server infrastructure capable of delivering seamless real-time experiences to a global audience.

GRA496.description:
The Graduation Thesis is an integrative experience that brings together various components of the undergraduate international business studies in a more applied setting and under a new perspective. It enables students to further their knowledge and skills in international business and related topics which they have found to be especially interesting or beneficial to them.

As part of the course, students will learn about all aspects of the process of developing and carrying out the graduation thesis and gain an understanding of standards and expectations needed to successfully complete their dissertation. This thesis project will be completed by a group of 3-5 students, however each student will defend the thesis individually in front of a thesis committee. Each group of students will be supported by a supervisor, who will provide them with essential guidance in conducting a research, writing a thesis in a formal format and defending their arguments in front of the examination board. 

The thesis' topic is concerned with such areas as (1) international business strategies, (2) contemporary issues of cross-cultural business management, (3) global entrepreneurship, (4) global human resource management - current practices and future trends, (5) FDI in Vietnam, (6) ethical issues in international business, (7) international trade in the current global geo-political landscape and (8) international business practices towards sustainability

GRA497.description:
Main objectives:
'As a course within the Media and Communication curriculum, the Capstone Project is comprehensive, allowing students to apply the combined knowledge acquired from earlier courses and projects to the production of more fully-realized work. The main objectives of the course are to:
- Exhibit an advanced understanding of the relationship between media and communication;
- Exhibit an advanced understanding of the theories of humanities and social science;
- Create a self-project as a media and communication professional; 
- Develop personal/ team work on a professional level of quality;
- Construct professional media and communication practices;
- Demonstrate proficiency in communication, presentation, and the necessary skills for professional practice, such as the capacity to organise and manage projects as well as collaborate effectively with others. This competency requires knowledge of organisational structures and work patterns in the fields of economics, media, and communication.
Description: 
- This course requires real-work projects completed by a group of 3-5 students, each student must defend their contribution to the group project individually in front of a professional committee/examination board.
- Students are strongly encouraged to form groups and actively seek their supervisor(s), who will provide the necessary guidance as they develop their projects from initial concepts or ideas to completion. 
- By the completion, students are expected to acquire a comprehensive understanding and skills in the field of media and communication.
The project consists of four (04) main phases:
(1) Research and development,
(2) Pre-implementation/Pre-production,
(3) Implementation/production, 
(4) Post-implementation/post-production, distribution (if applicable), and evaluation
Students are required to participate in and deliver progress reports to the department's professional committee at the CP Proposal completion stage. Students are expected to demonstrate a high level of professionalism when discussing, organising, presenting, and critiquing their work, as well as when implementing research strategies that contribute to the completion of the project in response to constructive feedback from supervisor(s) and professional committees.

Completion Criteria: 
- Progress on Project (04 reports): 40% 
- Final report/Production Book: 10%
- Project Defense: 50%

Overall Final Project Mark: 100%
Mark of each report must be >= 4/10
Final Report/Production Book >= 4/10
Oral Project Defense >= 5/10
Final Report/Production Book must be submitted before deadline
